problemText: What does register mean in writing? Choose the definition that matches what you learned in class.
choices: The specific pitch and volume a speaker produces when delivering words out loud to an audience
The official record or log that documents the names and contact details of attendees at a particular gathering or event
How formal or informal a piece of writing needs to be for its audience and purpose
The method by which a writer structures and arranges the sequence of paragraphs to guide readers from start to finish
hints: Think about the difference between writing a school report and texting a friend.
Register is about the level of formality you choose at the start and keep throughout.

problemText: Read this sentence from a thank-you letter to your grandmother: 'The gift was absolutely fire, no cap.' The rest of the letter uses warm, everyday words like 'so happy' and 'loved spending time with you.' Why is this sentence a problem in the letter?
choices: It is a sentence fragment and needs to be fixed with standard grammar
It does not tell the reader what gift you received from your grandmother
It is too short compared to the other sentences in the letter
It uses slang and casual filler words that do not match the warm but respectful register of the rest of the letter
hints: The lesson says a lapse can be a perfectly correct sentence — the problem is not grammar but register.
Look at what signals a casual register: slang, casual filler words, and exaggeration.

problemText: A student is writing a formal announcement about a field trip for the school website. Most sentences use careful, precise wording like 'Students will depart from the main entrance at 8:30 a.m.' and 'All participants must bring a packed lunch.' Which sentence would break the formal register of this announcement?
choices: Honestly, the aquarium is literally the coolest place ever, and you should totally go if you can.
Chaperones will monitor and assist students during the entire scheduled visit to the aquarium facility.
All permission slips must be completed, signed by a parent or guardian, and delivered by the deadline of Wednesday.
The transportation bus will arrive back at school by 3:00 p.m., ensuring students meet the afternoon dismissal schedule.
hints: Formal register uses precise vocabulary and no slang — look for casual filler words in the choices.
Which sentence uses words like 'honestly,' 'literally,' and 'totally' that do not fit a school announcement?

problemText: Read this short book review for a school assignment: 'The novel follows a young hero on a dangerous quest to save her village. The author builds tension throughout the story with sharp, suspenseful dialogue. We were literally so hyped while reading the last chapter because the ending was insane. The book teaches important lessons about courage and loyalty.' Identify the sentence that breaks the formal, informative tone and explain why it is the lapse.
choices: The first sentence is the lapse because it uses the word 'hero,' which is too casual for a formal review.
The third sentence is the lapse because it uses slang and casual filler words that do not match the careful, precise wording of the other sentences.
The second sentence is the lapse because it uses the word 'author,' which does not belong in a book review.
The fourth sentence is the lapse because it mentions lessons, which is not appropriate for a school assignment.
hints: First, read the other three sentences and decide what register most of the review is using.
Look for casual filler words and slang signals, then compare the sentence with the register that the rest of the piece established.

problemText: A student wrote this informal text to a friend about a weekend project: 'I finally finished painting my bedroom this weekend and it looks so awesome. We went to the store twice because we did not have enough paint for the first coat. Upon reflection, the acquisition of appropriate materials in advance would have facilitated the completion of said endeavor. I cannot wait to show you the finished room when you visit next month.' Which sentence is the lapse, and what should the student do to fix it?
choices: The first sentence is the lapse; rewrite it to use casual, everyday wording like the rest of the text.
The second sentence is the lapse; rewrite it to use slang and exaggeration to match the informal tone.
The third sentence is the lapse; rewrite it in casual, friendly wording that keeps the same information.
The fourth sentence is the lapse; rewrite it to match the formal vocabulary of the other sentences.
hints: Identify which register most of the text uses by reading the first, second, and fourth sentences together.
The lapse will have formal, stiff vocabulary that does not match the warm, casual wording the rest of the piece already established.

problemText: A student is revising a formal email to a museum director requesting a group visit. The student has identified this sentence as breaking the register: 'The field trip would be educational for our students and help them learn about art history, which would be sick.' Which of the following revisions best fixes the lapse by keeping the same information in the established formal register?
choices: The field trip would be educational for our students and help them learn about art history, and that sounds pretty good.
The field trip would help our sixth-grade students gain knowledge about art history because it is literally the best way to learn.
The field trip would teach our students about art history, and honestly, it would be really awesome for everyone.
The field trip would be an excellent educational opportunity that allows our students to deepen their understanding of art history.
hints: A proper fix replaces the slang word 'sick' with formal, precise vocabulary while preserving the core information about the field trip's educational value.
Check each choice: Does it remove the casual register completely and use careful word choice that matches a formal email to an official?

problemText: A nonrestrictive element is information that a sentence does not need in order to identify what it is talking about. Which sentence contains a nonrestrictive element that is correctly set off with commas?
choices: My best friend Marcus invited me to his birthday party.
My best friend, Marcus, invited me to his birthday party.
The student who finished first got a prize.
The cake which was chocolate tasted delicious.
hints: Use the removal test: cover 'Marcus' and read what is left. Does the sentence still point to the same person?
Remember that a nonrestrictive element sitting in the middle of a sentence needs a matching pair of marks on both sides.

problemText: Jordan has three younger brothers. One of them is named Tyler. Jordan wants to write a sentence about something Tyler did. Which sentence correctly punctuates the name to show that Tyler is one of several brothers?
choices: Jordan's brother, Tyler, scored the winning goal in the soccer game.
Jordan's brother — Tyler — scored the winning goal in the soccer game.
Jordan's brother Tyler scored the winning goal in the soccer game.
Jordan's brother, Tyler scored the winning goal in the soccer game.
hints: Apply the removal test: cover 'Tyler' and ask whether the sentence still tells you which brother did this.
Since Jordan has three brothers, the name Tyler is doing necessary identifying work. What punctuation does restrictive information need?

problemText: The school has only one cafeteria. A writer wants to add extra information about when it opens. Which sentence correctly sets off the nonrestrictive information with a matching pair of commas?
choices: The cafeteria opens at 7:00 a.m., which serves breakfast before school.
The cafeteria which opens at 7:00 a.m. serves breakfast before school.
The cafeteria which, opens at 7:00 a.m., serves breakfast before school.
The cafeteria, which opens at 7:00 a.m., serves breakfast before school.
hints: Cover the clause 'which opens at 7:00 a.m.' with your thumb. Does the remaining sentence still point to the same cafeteria?
When extra information sits in the middle of a sentence, it needs a comma before it and a comma after it.

problemText: A writer has written three sentences about a city park. Sentence 1: 'The park which has a new playground is a mile from my house.' Sentence 2: 'My favorite playground, the slide tower, is the tallest one in the city.' Sentence 3: 'The basketball court that has the best rim gets very crowded after school.' The writer learns that Sentence 2 is about the only playground the writer has ever called a favorite. Which of the following correctly describes which sentence is punctuated correctly for the facts given?
choices: Sentence 2 is correct because it uses a matching pair of commas to set off extra information; Sentence 1 needs commas around 'which has a new playground.'
Sentence 1 is correct because the playground is restrictive; Sentence 2 is wrong because 'the slide tower' is nonrestrictive but has only one comma.
Sentence 3 is correct because 'that has the best rim' is restrictive information; Sentence 2 needs dashes instead of commas.
Sentence 1 is correct as written; Sentence 3 needs parentheses because the court is the only one.
hints: For each sentence, use the removal test on the part in question. Does the sentence still identify the exact same thing without it?
Remember: a nonrestrictive element in the middle always needs a matching pair of marks, and opening with one comma but not closing with another leaves the element unpunctuated.

problemText: A writer is revising a sentence and wants to change the punctuation from commas to dashes to make the extra information stand out more forcefully. The current sentence is: 'The artist, who painted the mural downtown, is my neighbor.' Which revised sentence correctly uses a matching pair of dashes instead of commas?
choices: The artist — who painted the mural downtown is my neighbor.
The artist — who painted the mural downtown — is my neighbor.
The artist — who painted the mural downtown, is my neighbor.
The artist who painted the mural downtown — is my neighbor.
hints: Remember the pairing rule: use the SAME mark on both sides of the extra information, never open with one kind and close with another.
If commas worked on both sides of 'who painted the mural downtown,' then dashes should work the same way — one mark before the clause and one mark after it.

problemText: A student has written four sentences. The student knows that Sentence A has two sisters, Sentence B has only one cousin, Sentence C has one school, and Sentence D has multiple trophies won by the same person. Read each sentence and decide which one contains a punctuation error where extra information is concerned. Sentence A: 'My sister Elena loves to draw.' Sentence B: 'My cousin, who moved here last year, sits next to me in math class.' Sentence C: 'The school that offers the most sports programs is fifteen miles away.' Sentence D: 'The swimmer, Jorge, won three gold medals at the meet.'
choices: Sentence A — it should have commas around 'Elena' because the name identifies which sister
Sentence B — the clause 'who moved here last year' is restrictive and should have no commas
Sentence D — it needs a second comma after 'Jorge' to close off the appositive in the middle
Sentence C — the clause 'that offers the most sports programs' is nonrestrictive and should have commas
hints: Apply the removal test to each sentence. For Sentence A, cover 'Elena' — does the writer have two sisters, so the name must identify which one?
For Sentence D, check whether the name sits in the middle of the sentence. If it does, a mid-sentence nonrestrictive element needs a matching pair of marks, not just one.

problemText:
A complete sentence must have three parts. Which group of words is missing one of those three parts and is therefore a fragment?

Read each option and decide which one cannot stand on its own.
choices: It went off early in the morning.
The alarm went off early.
The alarm went off.
Because the alarm went off early.
hints: Look for a starter word like because, although, when, or since that leaves you waiting for more.
A fragment has a subject and verb but the starter word keeps the thought unfinished.

problemText:
Read this sentence and decide which problem it has.

"The skateboard ramp was closed, the park locked all the gates."
choices: It is a comma splice with two complete sentences joined by only a comma.
It is a fragment missing a subject.
It is a run-on with no punctuation between two complete sentences.
It is correct as written.
hints: Test each part before and after the comma to see if it has a subject, verb, and finished thought.
A comma by itself is not strong enough to hold two complete sentences apart.

problemText:
Which sentence is written correctly and needs no fix?

Consider whether each one has a subject, verb, and finished thought, or if it has two complete sentences joined incorrectly.
choices: After the movie ended we went for ice cream.
We went for ice cream because the movie ended.
The movie ended, we went for ice cream.
The movie ended we went for ice cream.
hints: Check for starter words that need a comma only when they come first.
Look for a comma between two complete sentences — that is a splice unless there is a joining word too.

problemText:
Read this pair of sentences. One has an error and one does not.

Sentence 1: "Since the buses were delayed, the morning announcements started late."
Sentence 2: "Since the buses were delayed. The morning announcements started late."

Which sentence is correct, and what is wrong with the other one?
choices: Sentence 2 is correct because it uses a period to separate two independent thoughts about the buses and the announcements.
Sentence 2 is correct; Sentence 1 is a run-on because it has a comma between two complete sentences.
Sentence 1 is correct; Sentence 2 is a fragment because a period cannot follow a starter word without a complete sentence attached.
Sentence 1 is correct; Sentence 2 is incorrect because the dependent clause "Since the buses were delayed" is left hanging without a complete thought to complete its meaning.
hints: A starter word like since must be attached to a complete sentence; a period separates them instead.
Test the first part of Sentence 2 — does it have a finished thought, or is it waiting for more?

problemText:
Fix this sentence three different ways. "The computer crashed my project was gone."

Which answer shows all three legal fixes for this error?
choices: Delete some words, or use a dash, or add a noun to the first part.
Add a period, or use a semicolon, or use a comma and a starter word like because.
Use a comma, or flip the order, or add a joining word.
Add a period, or use a semicolon, or use a comma and a joining word like so.
hints: Remember the three legal fixes: period, semicolon, or comma plus a joining word (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so).
A joining word connects two complete sentences; a starter word begins an unfinished thought that needs to attach to a complete sentence.

problemText:
Read these four attempts to fix the fragment. "Although the concert tickets sold out in minutes."

Each writer tried a different strategy. Only one actually fixes the error. Which one is correct and works as a legal repair?
choices: Although the concert tickets sold out in minutes, fans are already planning for next year's show.
Although the concert tickets sold out in minutes; fans are already planning for next year's show.
Although the concert tickets sold out in minutes. Fans are already planning for next year's show.
Although the concert tickets sold out in minutes, but fans are already planning for next year's show.
hints: A starter word must be attached to a complete sentence with a comma when it comes first; not separated by a period or semicolon.
Do not use both a starter word and a joining word in the same fix — that creates a different error.

problemText: What does it mean when a paragraph has sentence variety? Which statement describes what sentence variety changes and what it does not change?
choices: It changes the shape of sentences by mixing their length and openers, but keeps all the facts and meaning exactly the same.
It changes the meaning of the sentences and adds new facts to make writing more interesting.
It removes short sentences entirely and replaces them with longer, fancier words throughout the entire paragraph.
It changes which facts appear in the paragraph and reorganizes events so the reader stays more focused.
hints: Look for the choice that mentions shape rather than meaning or facts.
The lesson emphasized that sentence variety changes how sentences sound and look, not what they say.

problemText:
Read this paragraph from a student's journal:

"I woke up early. I grabbed my soccer gear. I met my friends at the field."

What is the repeated pattern a reader would notice first before understanding the content of these sentences?
choices: The word 'early' is mentioned in the first sentence.
All three sentences have the exact same opening word, 'I'.
Each sentence is about a different time of day.
The sentences are in alphabetical order by their second word.
hints: The lesson taught that the most noticeable repeated pattern is what word or phrase appears at the start of each sentence.
Look only at the first word of each sentence in the paragraph.

problemText:
A student is revising two sentences for the class newsletter:

"The gym door was locked. The students waited outside."

The student wants to state the relationship between what happened first and what happened second. Which revision uses a connector to show that relationship without adding or changing any facts?
choices: The gym door was very locked, and the students definitely waited outside.
The gym door was locked. The students were waiting outside in the cold.
Since the gym door was locked, the students waited outside.
The locked gym door made the students wait outside for a long time.
hints: Find the choice that adds a connector word like 'when,' 'after,' 'because,' or 'so' to state the connection.
The connector should explain why the students waited, not just make the sentences longer or change the wording.

problemText:
A paragraph for the school blog reads:

"The rain started during lunch. The rain flooded the playground. The principal moved everyone indoors. The principal sent an email home to families."

What are the two specific fixes a revision must make to truly improve this paragraph's sentence variety? Choose the answer that names both fixes needed.
choices: Replace the repeated 'The rain' opener by combining those two sentences, and replace the repeated 'The principal' opener by giving at least one of those sentences a different starting word.
Move the word 'the' to a different position in the first sentence and change 'moved' to 'shifted' in the third sentence.
Delete every other sentence so the paragraph is shorter and easier to read.
Combine the two sentences that start with 'The rain' and give at least one other sentence a different opener instead of starting with 'The principal'.
hints: Remember the two testable fixes: removing a repeated opener (three or more times in a row) and adding a connector that states a relationship.
Look for which choice identifies both a repeated opening word and a way to address it, plus gives a different opener to another sentence.

problemText:
A student wrote this paragraph for a story:

"The storm arrived suddenly. The storm knocked down tree branches. It scattered leaves everywhere."

The student's teacher says the paragraph is 'correct but still choppy.' What revision would fix the choppiness while keeping every single fact from the original sentences?
choices: The sudden storm knocked down tree branches and scattered leaves everywhere.
The storm arrived suddenly and knocked down very many tree branches, scattering leaves in every direction.
When the storm arrived suddenly, it knocked down tree branches and scattered leaves everywhere.
A heavy and powerful storm arrived, knocked down branches, and sent leaves all over.
hints: The repeated opener 'The storm' appears in the first two sentences; combine them to remove that repetition.
Check that your choice keeps all four original facts (the storm, suddenly arriving, knocking down branches, and scattering leaves) without adding new details.

problemText:
A student rewrote a paragraph this way:

Original: "We found a turtle by the pond. We called the wildlife center. They sent a specialist."

Revision: "When we found a turtle by the pond, we called the wildlife center, and they sent a specialist."

The student claims this revision fixes the choppiness. Using what the lesson taught about testable fixes, explain whether this student's claim is correct. Which statement accurately describes what the revision does?
choices: The revision fails to address choppiness because it keeps the subject 'we' at the start of multiple clauses and does not combine the sentences properly into one.
The revision fixes the choppiness by combining sentences and adding the connector 'when' that states the timing relationship, even though no single opener was repeated three times in a row.
The revision creates a serious sentence error because it combines three independent sentences with only commas and loses the original meaning of the events.
The revision improves only slightly because it adds 'when' but then introduces another connector 'and' that makes the sentence confusing instead of clearer.
hints: A testable fix does one of two things: it removes a repeated opener (three or more in a row), or it adds a connector that states a relationship between ideas.
Even though 'we' is not repeated four times in a row, the revision still uses 'when' to state when the events happened—this is one of the two valid reasons to revise.
